subject: economics
book: Statistics for Economics; Introductory Microeconomics (NCERT, rationalised)

concepts.text: Economics as the study of everyday economic activity: people acting as consumers, sellers, producers, employees and employers
Identify the economic role of a person (e.g. shopkeeper = seller, doctor = service producer, taxi driver = service provider)
We cannot get something for nothing: unlimited wants versus limited income force choices at given prices
Scarcity as the root of all economic problems; resources have alternative uses, so society must choose
Everyday signs of scarcity: queues, crowded buses, shortages, land usable for food or cash crops
Three core branches: consumption, production and distribution (how national income splits into wages, profit, interest, rent)
Formal definition: economics studies how society uses scarce resources with alternative uses to produce and distribute goods
Modern economics also studies poverty, inequality, education, jobs and disasters, which needs statistical data
Activity type: list your wants, which remain unmet, and the kinds of scarcity you face and why
Economic facts expressed as numbers are economic data
Chain from data to analysis (finding causes of a problem) to policy (measures to solve it)
Without data there can be no analysis or policy, which links economics and statistics
Statistics in the plural sense (numerical data) and singular sense (methods of collection, presentation, analysis, interpretation)
Quantitative data: characteristics measured as numbers (e.g. rice output in million tonnes)
Qualitative data: attributes not measured numerically (gender, health, skill), often described in degrees
Stages of a statistical study: collect, organise and present (tables, diagrams, graphs), summarise, analyse, interpret
Classify given characteristics (beauty, intelligence, income, marks, singing ability) as qualitative or quantitative
Statistics states economic facts precisely; exact figures are more convincing than vague statements
Condenses mass data into a few summary measures such as averages
Finds and tests relationships between economic variables (price-demand, income-consumption, government spending-prices)
Helps forecast future values and plan policy (e.g. projected consumption, oil imports)
Helps identify causes of problems and evaluate whether a policy is working
Statistical methods are no substitute for common sense: misuse of averages (family crossing a river of 'average depth')
Limitations of statistics: deals with aggregates not individuals, can be misused or misinterpreted, needs care in use
True/false statements on the scope of statistics (quantitative and qualitative, use in solving problems)
List activities seen at a market or bus stand and pick out the economic ones
Give examples of governments using statistical data to make development policy
Explain with examples that wants are unlimited and resources limited; how you would choose which wants to satisfy
Comment, with everyday examples, on why statistical methods cannot replace common sense
Data as values of variables; each value is an observation; data help explain economic problems
Primary data: collected first-hand by the investigator for the enquiry
Secondary data: already collected and processed by another agency; saves time and cost
The same data are primary for the collector and secondary for later users
Choosing between primary and secondary data depending on purpose, time and money

sections.name: 2.3 How do we Collect the Data?

concepts.text: A survey collects information from individuals; preparing the instrument (questionnaire or interview schedule)
Rules for a good questionnaire: short, clear, logically ordered from general to specific, precise wording
Questions to avoid: ambiguous wording, double negatives, leading questions, hints at an answer, calculations
Closed-ended questions: two-way (yes/no) and multiple-choice; easy to score, hard to frame
Open-ended questions: allow free answers; hard to compare and interpret
Personal interview method: face-to-face, allows clarification and observation; costly, slow, interviewer may influence answers
Mailing questionnaire method: cheap, wide coverage, reaches remote areas; low response, no clarification; online/SMS surveys
Telephone interview method: cheaper and quicker than personal visits; limited to people with phones, no face-to-face cues
Comparing modes of data collection: advantages and disadvantages table
Pilot survey: small trial run to test the questionnaire, instructions, enumerators, and cost/time of the main survey
Activity type: choose a suitable mode of data collection for a given situation and justify it
Population (universe): all items under study; census (complete enumeration) covers every unit
Census of India conducted every 10 years; population growth trend 1901-2011
Sample: a representative part of the population; cheaper, faster, can give reasonably accurate results
Advantages of a sample survey over a census; when a census is preferable
Random sampling: every unit has an equal chance of selection; lottery method and random number tables / computer
Sampling frame: list of all units of the population from which the sample is drawn
Exit polls as an application of sampling and why they can go wrong
Non-random sampling: judgement, convenience, purposive and quota sampling; units do not have equal chances, risk of bias
Identify population, sample and variable in a given study (e.g. 200 farms, 50 surveyed)
Count possible samples (e.g. ways of choosing 3 students from 10)
Sampling error: difference between a sample estimate and the true population value; falls as sample size rises
Numerical illustration: population mean of farmers' incomes vs sample mean gives sampling error
Non-sampling errors: arise in both census and sample; harder to control
Types of non-sampling error: sampling bias, non-response error, errors in data acquisition (recording/measurement mistakes)
Compare which error is more serious and why
Main national data agencies: Census of India, NSSO/NSS, CSO, Registrar General of India, DGCIS, Labour Bureau
Census of India: most complete demographic record, decennial since 1881, first after independence in 1951
NSSO surveys in rounds on socio-economic topics (consumer spending, employment, health); results in reports and the journal Sarvekshana
Other secondary sources: Economic Survey, RBI publications, international bodies
Frame multiple-choice and two-way questions on given topics
Critique badly framed questions for bias, leading wording, double negatives or ambiguity
Design a questionnaire for a product survey (e.g. popularity of a noodle brand)
True/false on sources of data, telephone surveys, secondary data, non-random bias and non-sampling errors
Explain the lottery method and random number tables; judge whether lottery always gives a random sample; census vs sample
Classification brings order to raw data so it can be analysed (kabadiwala sorting analogy)
Classes must follow a clear criterion
Raw (unclassified) data: large, disorganised and hard to analyse; finding highest value or average is tedious
Chronological (temporal) classification: by time; produces a time series
Spatial (geographical) classification: by place such as country, state or district
Qualitative classification: by attributes (gender, marital status), including manifold classification
Quantitative classification: by measurable characteristics (marks, height, income) into classes
Relative frequency: class frequency as a proportion or percentage of total frequency
Variable: a characteristic whose value changes; contrast with attribute
Continuous variable: can take any value in an interval, including fractions (height, weight, time)
Discrete variable: takes only certain values, changing in jumps (number of students, cars)
Classify given variables (area, temperature, dice number, population, rainfall, age) as continuous or discrete
Frequency distribution: shows how values of a variable are distributed across classes with frequencies
Class, class frequency, class limits (lower and upper), class interval / width (upper minus lower limit)
Class mark (mid-point) = (upper limit + lower limit) / 2; represents the class in calculations
Range = largest value minus smallest value
Frequency curve: plotting frequencies against class marks
Deciding equal vs unequal class intervals (unequal when data have a very wide range or cluster)
Number of classes (usually 6-15) and the formula number of classes = range / class width
Choosing clear class limits; open-ended classes and why they are avoided
Tally marking: counting frequencies in groups of five
Exclusive method: upper limit excluded from the class (e.g. 10-20, 20-30)
Inclusive method: both limits included (e.g. 10-19, 20-29)
Adjustment of inclusive classes: subtract half the gap from lower limits and add to upper limits to make classes continuous
Loss of information when data are grouped: values replaced by the class mark
Frequency distribution with unequal classes and why it can represent data better
Frequency array: frequency distribution for a discrete variable (e.g. household size)
Bivariate (two-way) frequency distribution: joint frequencies of two variables in a table (sales vs advertisement expenditure)
Reading a cell of a bivariate table; univariate vs bivariate distribution
MCQ on class mid-point, range, bivariate distribution
Construct a frequency distribution from raw data with suitable classes and answer count questions (below/above/between values)
Build a frequency array from survey responses or from letter counts of words
Construct an inclusive frequency distribution with a given class width
Explain advantages of classification and argue whether classified data are better than raw data
Three forms of presentation: textual (descriptive), tabular and diagrammatic
Textual presentation: data described in sentences; suitable for small data; can emphasise points but needs full reading
Table: data arranged in rows and columns; each box is a cell
Qualitative classification in tables (by attribute, e.g. literacy by sex and location)
Quantitative classification in tables (by class limits, e.g. age groups)
Temporal classification in tables (by year)
Spatial classification in tables (by place, e.g. export shares by country)

sections.name: 4.4 Tabulation of Data and Parts of a Table

concepts.text: One-way, two-way and three-way tables depending on number of characteristics
Parts of a table: table number, title, captions (column headings), stubs (row headings)
Parts of a table: body, unit of measurement, source, note
Rounding large figures and stating the unit; rules of a good table
Activity type: convert a passage of text data (e.g. census facts) into a table
Diagrams give quick understanding; less exact than tables
Simple bar diagram: equal-width, equally spaced bars with heights showing values; for discrete variables, attributes and non-frequency data
Multiple bar diagram: two or more bars side by side to compare data sets (e.g. literacy in 2001 vs 2011)
Component (sub-divided) bar diagram: bar split into parts; percentage component bars with total height 100
Pie diagram: circle divided into sectors; angle = percentage x 3.6 degrees (or value/total x 360)
Calculate sector angles from data and draw a pie chart
Histogram: adjacent rectangles on class intervals, area proportional to frequency; only for continuous data
Histogram with unequal classes: use frequency density (frequency / class width) for heights
Locating the mode graphically from a histogram
Histogram vs bar diagram: width matters in a histogram, bars have gaps and equal widths
Frequency polygon: join mid-points of histogram tops, close at zero-frequency classes at both ends; or plot frequency against class marks
Frequency curve: smooth freehand curve through frequency polygon points
Less-than ogive: cumulative frequency plotted against upper class limits; rising curve
More-than ogive: cumulative frequency plotted against lower class limits; falling curve
Median from the intersection of less-than and more-than ogives
Arithmetic line graph (time series graph): time on x-axis, value on y-axis; shows trend, cycles and seasonality
Multiple line graph comparing two series (e.g. exports and imports of India)
MCQ / true-false on bar width, histogram for continuous data, mode from histogram, median from ogives
Choose the most suitable diagram for given data (monthly rainfall, religious composition, cost components)
Tabulate given data, choose and draw an appropriate diagram, and justify the choice
Plot sectoral growth rates as multiple time series graphs
Average: a single value representing the whole data set; three averages studied are mean, median and mode
Geometric and harmonic means exist but are outside this chapter
Arithmetic mean = sum of observations / number of observations
Ungrouped data: direct method, mean = sum X / N
Ungrouped data: assumed mean method, mean = A + sum d / N where d = X - A
Ungrouped data: step deviation method, mean = A + (sum d' / N) x c where d' = (X - A)/c
Discrete series: direct method, mean = sum fX / sum f
Discrete series: assumed mean and step deviation methods using fd and fd'
Continuous series: use class mid-points; direct, assumed mean and step deviation methods
Mean for inclusive, exclusive and unequal class intervals and from cumulative (more than / less than) frequency tables
Property: sum of deviations of observations from the mean is zero
Property: mean is affected by extreme values
Weighted arithmetic mean = sum wX / sum w; weights reflect relative importance (e.g. budget shares)
Finding a missing frequency when the mean is given
Activity type: check how the mean changes when observations change or an extreme value replaces one item
Median: positional middle value of ordered data; splits data into two equal halves; not affected by extreme values
Ungrouped data: median = size of (N+1)/2 th item; average of two middle items when N is even
Discrete series: locate (N+1)/2 th item with cumulative frequency
Continuous series: median class contains N/2 th item; median = L + ((N/2 - c.f.)/f) x h
Median from less-than cumulative frequency data
Quartiles Q1, Q2, Q3 divide ordered data into four equal parts; Q1 = (N+1)/4 th item, Q3 = 3(N+1)/4 th item [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Percentiles divide data into 100 parts; P50 equals the median; meaning of a percentile rank [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Using median and quartiles to answer income-share questions (top 25%, bottom 50%) [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Mode: most frequently occurring value; unimodal, bimodal, multimodal or no mode
Discrete series: value with the highest frequency
Continuous series: modal class; mode = L + (D1/(D1 + D2)) x h
Mode formula needs equal, exclusive class intervals; convert cumulative/inclusive data first
Mode suits qualitative data and choices like shoe or garment sizes; can be located graphically

sections.name: 5.5 Relative Position of Mean, Median and Mode

concepts.text: Median lies between mean and mode; in a symmetric distribution all three are equal
Choosing the appropriate average for a purpose (sizes, wages, open-ended classes, ratios)
Comparing merits and limits of mean, median and mode
Choose the suitable average for given situations
MCQ / true-false on deviations from mean, positional averages, upper quartile, effect of extremes
Compute mean from ungrouped data and from more-than cumulative frequencies
Compute median from less-than cumulative data; compute mean, median and mode for a grouped distribution
Find a missing frequency given the mean, then the median
Correlation studies whether and how two variables move together: existence, direction and strength of relationship
Cause-and-effect relationships (price and demand) vs coincidental relationships
Spurious correlation due to a third variable (ice-cream sales and drowning both driven by temperature)
Correlation measures covariation, not causation; assumes a linear relationship
Positive correlation: variables move in the same direction (income and consumption)
Negative correlation: variables move in opposite directions (price and quantity demanded)
Scatter diagram: plot paired values as points to see the relationship visually
Reading scatter diagrams: upward pattern positive, downward negative, no pattern zero, points on a line perfect correlation
Scatter diagram can reveal non-linear relationships; does not give a numerical value

sections.name: 6.3 Techniques: Karl Pearson's Coefficient of Correlation

concepts.text: Karl Pearson's coefficient (product moment / simple correlation) measures linear relationship
Covariance cov(X,Y) = sum (X - Xbar)(Y - Ybar) / N; standard deviations as square roots of variances
Formula r = sum xy / (N sigma_x sigma_y), using deviations from actual means
Formula r = sum xy / (sqrt(sum x^2) sqrt(sum y^2))
Direct (actual values) formula r = [N sum XY - sum X sum Y] / [sqrt(N sum X^2 - (sum X)^2) sqrt(N sum Y^2 - (sum Y)^2)]
Property: r is a pure number without units; preferred over covariance for this reason
Property: -1 <= r <= +1; a value outside this range means a calculation error
Property: r is unaffected by change of origin and scale
Interpreting r = +1, -1, 0, close to 1 and close to 0; r = 0 means no linear relation, not independence
Step deviation method for r: U = (X - A)/B, V = (Y - C)/D
Worked example type: correlation between years of schooling and farm yield; price index and money supply
Common sense in interpreting r (doctors and epidemic deaths example)
When to use rank correlation: attributes not measurable (beauty, honesty), only ranks available, extreme values, monotonic non-linear data
Formula r_s = 1 - 6 sum D^2 / (n^3 - n), D = difference in ranks
Case 1: ranks given (e.g. judges in a beauty contest; which pair of judges agree most)
Case 2: ranks not given: assign ranks to marks first, then apply formula
Case 3: repeated (tied) ranks: assign average rank; correction factor (m^3 - m)/12 added for each tie
Rank correlation lies between -1 and +1; generally less precise than Pearson's r because it uses less information
MCQ on unit and range of r, meaning of positive and zero r, measure for any type of relationship
Conceptual: why r over covariance; can r lie outside -1 to 1; does correlation imply causation
Compute Pearson's r for given paired data (father-son heights; symmetric data giving r = 0; perfectly linear data giving r = 1)
Compute rank correlation with and without tied ranks; practical activity on prices or classmates' heights
Index number: device measuring average change in a group of related variables over time or place
Base period: comparison period with index set at 100; reading an index value (250 = 2.5 times base)
Price index vs quantity index (production, employment, construction)
Simple aggregative price index = (sum P1 / sum P0) x 100; drawbacks: unit differences and equal weights
Weighted aggregative index using quantities as weights
Laspeyres price index = (sum P1 q0 / sum P0 q0) x 100 (base-year quantities)
Paasche price index = (sum P1 q1 / sum P0 q1) x 100 (current-year quantities)
Laspeyres and Paasche differ only in the weights used; interpreting each
Price relative = (P1 / P0) x 100
Simple average of price relatives = (1/n) sum (P1/P0 x 100)
Weighted average of price relatives = sum W R / sum W, with base-year expenditure shares as weights
Worked example type: compute Laspeyres, Paasche and weighted relative indices for 4 commodities
Consumer price index (cost of living index): average change in retail prices of a consumption basket
CPI computed by weighted relatives method (CPI = sum WR / sum W); wage adjustment by excess over 100
Different CPIs: industrial workers, agricultural labourers, rural labourers, CPI rural/urban/combined (base 2012)
CPI-combined major groups and weights; Consumer Food Price Index
Wholesale price index: general price level of goods at wholesale; no services; base 2011-12; weights of primary articles, fuel, manufactures
Headline vs core inflation
Index of industrial production: quantity index, Laspeyres formula with value-added weights; sectoral and use-based weights; eight core industries
Human Development Index as a composite index (mention)
Sensex: BSE index of 30 stocks, base 1978-79, benchmark of the stock market

sections.name: 7.5 Issues in Construction of an Index Number

concepts.text: Clear purpose; selection of representative items for the target group
Choice of base year: normal year, not too distant; base revision
Choice of formula and reliability of data
Uses of CPI: wage negotiation, income/price policy, rent control, taxation
Uses of WPI: deflating aggregates like national income; measuring inflation
Inflation rate = (X_t - X_{t-1}) / X_{t-1} x 100 from a price index
Purchasing power of money = 1 / cost of living index
Real wage = (money wage / CPI) x 100
Salary needed to keep the same standard of living = base salary x CPI / 100
Uses of IIP, agricultural production index and Sensex
MCQ on weighted index, base-year weights, CPI scope, inflation measure
Short answers: need for index numbers, desirable base period, why different CPIs, price vs quantity index
Compute a cost of living index from weights and prices
Find required salary adjustment from CPI; find food's weight from group indices; weighted average tax (GST) rate
Interpret IIP / CPI / WPI tables and comment on comparability across bases
Purpose of a project: apply statistical tools to study an economic issue and suggest improvements
Step 1: identify the problem or area of study and set clear objectives
Step 2: choose the target group (population) whose members will be surveyed
Step 3: collect data: primary (questionnaire / interview schedule, personal, postal, phone, email) or secondary; choose sampling method
Covering letter for postal questionnaires; using secondary data when time or money is short
Step 4: organise and present data in tables and suitable diagrams (bar, pie, histogram)
Step 5: analyse and interpret with averages, correlation (and dispersion measures) [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Step 6: draw conclusions, forecast prospects and suggest policies
Step 7: bibliography listing all secondary sources used
Role-based project prompts: transport advisor, bank-loan proposal for a cottage unit, advertising effect on sales
Role-based project prompts: literacy and dropouts, overcharging above MRP, drinking water, women's employment
Role-based project prompts: health and sanitation, food adulteration, immunisation, household saving habits, farm problems
Designing a questionnaire for a consumer survey: demographics, income, occupation, brand use, satisfaction, preferences, media
Presenting age distribution with a table and bar diagram; family size with a histogram
Frequency distribution of income and spending with mean (assumed mean / step deviation)
Occupational status with a pie diagram; brand preference and basis of choice counts
Interpreting results: satisfaction by brand, ingredient preferences, media influence
Writing the concluding note of a project report from the findings
Individuals produce, exchange and consume to meet needs; society's resources are limited
Scarcity forces choices about how to allocate resources
What to produce and in what quantities
How to produce: choice of technique (labour-intensive vs capital-intensive)
For whom to produce: distribution of output among people
Production possibility set: all output combinations possible with given resources and technology
Production possibility frontier (PPF): combinations obtained when resources are fully and efficiently used
Points inside the PPF show under-used or wasted resources; points outside are unattainable
Opportunity cost: the amount of one good given up to produce one more unit of another
Marginal rate of transformation / increasing opportunity cost explains the concave shape of the PPF
Worked table type: corn-cotton production possibilities; compute opportunity cost and plot the PPF
Shifts of the PPF due to growth of resources or technology; rotation when technology changes for one good
Centrally planned economy: government makes key decisions on production, exchange and distribution
Market economy: decisions coordinated by prices in markets; market as an arrangement for free exchange, not just a place
Price signals: rising demand raises price and induces more supply
Mixed economy: combination of market and government roles (as in India)
Positive economics: describes how economic mechanisms actually work (what is)
Normative economics: evaluates whether outcomes are desirable (what ought to be)
Classify given statements as positive or normative
Microeconomics: behaviour of individual agents and price/quantity determination in individual markets
Macroeconomics: economy-wide aggregates such as total output, employment, price level, growth and inflation
Explain the central problems; define production possibility set and PPF; distinguish planned and market economies
Distinguish positive and normative analysis, and micro and macro economics
Two-good model and consumption bundles written as (x1, x2)
Utility: want-satisfying power of a good; subjective, varies with person, place and time
Cardinal approach: utility measured in numbers (utils)
Total utility (TU) and marginal utility MU_n = TU_n - TU_(n-1); TU = sum of MUs
Law of diminishing marginal utility
Relationship of TU and MU: TU rises while MU positive, TU maximum when MU = 0, TU falls when MU negative
Consumer's equilibrium with one good (MU = price) and two goods (MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y, equi-marginal rule)
Derivation of a downward-sloping demand curve from diminishing MU
Ordinal approach: consumer only ranks bundles
Indifference curve: bundles giving equal satisfaction; indifference schedule
Marginal rate of substitution MRS = |delta x2 / delta x1|; diminishing MRS
Convexity of indifference curves; straight-line IC for perfect substitutes
Monotonic preferences: more of at least one good with no less of the other is preferred
Indifference map: higher curves give higher satisfaction
Properties of ICs: slope downward, higher IC higher utility, two ICs never intersect (with proof by contradiction)
Budget set: all bundles affordable at given prices and income, p1x1 + p2x2 <= M
Budget line p1x1 + p2x2 = M; intercepts M/p1 and M/p2; slope -p1/p2
Why the budget line slopes downward; price ratio as market rate of exchange
Shift of budget line with change in income (parallel shift)
Rotation of budget line with change in one price; effect of changing both prices and income
Numericals: write the budget equation, find intercepts and slope, list affordable integer bundles, find income from a bundle
Consumer's equilibrium under IC approach: highest IC tangent to the budget line, MRS = p1/p2
Adjustment when MRS > or < price ratio
Demand: quantity a consumer is willing and able to buy at a price; demand function and determinants
Demand schedule and demand curve; law of demand
Deriving the demand curve from ICs and budget line
Substitution effect and income effect of a price change
Normal goods (demand rises with income) and inferior goods (demand falls with income); Giffen goods
Substitutes and complements and cross-price effects on demand
Shifts in the demand curve due to income, prices of related goods, tastes and preferences
Movement along vs shift of the demand curve (change in quantity demanded vs change in demand)
Market demand: horizontal summation of individual demand curves/schedules
Numerical: add linear individual demand functions, including piecewise ranges
Price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price; usually stated as absolute value
Percentage (proportionate) method: e_D = (delta Q / Q) x (P / delta P)
Elastic, inelastic and unitary elastic demand; perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic cases
Elasticity along a linear demand curve: zero at quantity axis, unitary at mid-point, infinite at price axis
Geometric (point) method: elasticity = lower segment / upper segment of the demand line
Rectangular hyperbola demand curve has unitary elasticity throughout
Factors determining elasticity: nature of good, availability of close substitutes (also share in budget, habits, time)
Total expenditure method: expenditure rises/falls/constant with price changes for inelastic/elastic/unitary demand
Numericals: compute elasticity from price-quantity changes; forecast quantity change from given elasticity; infer elasticity from expenditure change
Production function: maximum output from given inputs with given technology, q = f(L, K)
Reading an output table for different labour-capital combinations
Isoquant: input combinations giving the same output; downward sloping; higher isoquant higher output [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]

sections.name: 3.2 The Short Run and the Long Run

concepts.text: Short run: at least one factor fixed; long run: all factors variable
Periods defined by input flexibility, not calendar time

sections.name: 3.3 Total Product, Average Product and Marginal Product

concepts.text: Total product (TP): output as one variable input changes, others fixed
Average product AP = TP / L
Marginal product MP = delta TP / delta L, or TP_L - TP_(L-1)
TP = sum of MPs; AP as average of MPs up to that point
Numericals: compute AP and MP from TP; TP and MP from AP; TP and AP from MP

sections.name: 3.4 Law of Diminishing Marginal Product and Law of Variable Proportions

concepts.text: Law of variable proportions / returns to a factor: MP first rises, then falls (and can become negative)
Reasons: better factor proportions first, then crowding of the fixed factor
Three phases: increasing, diminishing and negative returns to a factor

sections.name: 3.5 Shapes of TP, MP and AP Curves

concepts.text: TP rises at an increasing rate, then a diminishing rate, reaches maximum when MP = 0
MP and AP are inverse-U shaped
MP cuts AP at AP's maximum; AP rises when MP > AP and falls when MP < AP
Constant, increasing and decreasing returns to scale when all inputs rise in the same proportion [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Cobb-Douglas production function q = x1^a x2^b; returns to scale from a + b [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Numericals: compute output from given production functions [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Cost function: least cost of producing each output level
Total fixed cost, total variable cost, TC = TFC + TVC
AFC = TFC/q, AVC = TVC/q, AC (SAC) = TC/q = AFC + AVC
Marginal cost SMC = delta TC / delta q = delta TVC / delta q; TVC = sum of MCs
Shapes: TFC horizontal; TVC and TC rise, TC parallel to TVC
AFC is a rectangular hyperbola falling continuously
SMC, AVC and SAC are U-shaped; reason (variable proportions)
SMC cuts AVC and SAC from below at their minimum points; minimum SAC lies to the right of minimum AVC
Gap between SAC and AVC equals AFC and narrows with output
Numericals: complete cost schedules from TC data or from SMC with given TFC
Long run costs: LRAC and LRMC; no fixed costs in the long run [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
U-shaped LRAC linked to returns to scale; LRMC cuts LRAC at its minimum [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]

sections.name: Revenue concepts (CBSE Unit 6; printed in Ch 4 of the book)

concepts.text: Total revenue TR = p x q; average revenue AR = TR/q = price; marginal revenue MR = delta TR / delta q
Relationship of TR, AR and MR when price is constant (AR = MR, TR a straight line from origin)
Numericals: complete TR, AR, MR schedules

chapters.title: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition

concepts.text: Large number of buyers and sellers; homogeneous product
Free entry and exit; perfect information
Firm is a price taker: faces a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve
TR = p x q is a straight line through the origin with slope p
Price line = AR = MR = demand curve for a price-taking firm
Numerical: TR and MR table at a fixed price (candle boxes example)
Profit = TR - TC
Condition 1: price equals marginal cost (MR = MC)
Condition 2: MC must be non-decreasing (rising) at the chosen output
Condition 3 short run: price must cover minimum AVC, else shut down (loss limited to TFC)
Condition 3 long run: price must cover minimum LRAC, else the firm exits
Graphical profit-maximising output and profit/loss rectangle using price, SAC and SMC
Numericals: find profit at each output and the profit-maximising output from TR/TC tables
Short run supply curve: rising part of SMC from minimum AVC upward; zero output below minimum AVC
Long run supply curve: rising part of LRMC from minimum LRAC upward
Shut-down point: minimum AVC (short run), minimum LRAC (long run)
Normal profit: minimum profit to stay in business, treated as part of cost (opportunity cost)
Super-normal profit; break-even point where price = minimum AC
Opportunity cost as the return from the next best alternative

sections.name: 4.5 Determinants of a Firm's Supply Curve

concepts.text: Technological progress lowers MC and shifts supply rightward
Rise in input prices raises MC and shifts supply leftward
Unit (per-unit) tax raises cost curves and shifts supply leftward
Supply schedule; movement along vs shift of supply curve (CBSE: determinants of supply)
Market supply: horizontal summation of firms' supply curves
Kinks due to different shut-down prices of firms
Effect of change in the number of firms on market supply
Numericals: add supply schedules/functions of two or more firms (including identical firms)
Price elasticity of supply = % change in quantity supplied / % change in price
Percentage method numericals (e.g. cricket balls); find new quantity from given elasticity
Geometric method for straight-line supply: e_S > 1 if line meets price axis, = 1 through origin, < 1 if it meets quantity axis
Perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic supply
Market equilibrium: plans of buyers and sellers match; quantity demanded = quantity supplied
Excess demand (demand > supply below equilibrium price) and excess supply (above it)
Invisible hand: price rises under excess demand and falls under excess supply until equilibrium

sections.name: 5.1.1 Market Equilibrium: Fixed Number of Firms

concepts.text: Equilibrium price and quantity at intersection of market demand and supply curves
Algebraic equilibrium from linear demand and supply functions (e.g. qD = 200 - p, qS = 120 + p)
Excess demand and excess supply functions at non-equilibrium prices
Wage determination in a perfectly competitive labour market: w = MRP_L = VMP_L; labour demand and supply [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Rightward/leftward shift of demand: price and quantity both rise/fall
Rightward/leftward shift of supply: price falls/rises, quantity rises/falls
Causes of shifts: income, related goods' prices, tastes, number of consumers; input prices, technology, number of firms
Simultaneous shifts in the same direction: quantity change certain, price change ambiguous
Simultaneous shifts in opposite directions: price change certain, quantity change ambiguous
Diagram drawing for all four simultaneous-shift cases
Numerical: new equilibrium after a supply shift or a per-unit tax

sections.name: 5.1.2 Market Equilibrium: Free Entry and Exit

concepts.text: With free entry and exit, price settles at minimum average cost; firms earn only normal profit [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Equilibrium number of firms = market quantity / output per firm [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Demand shifts under free entry: price unchanged, quantity and number of firms change [in book; not listed in CBSE 2026-27 syllabus]
Price ceiling: legal maximum price below equilibrium; creates excess demand (shortage)
Consequences of price ceiling: rationing via ration/fair price shops, queues, black markets
Price floor: legal minimum price above equilibrium; creates excess supply (surplus)
Examples of price floor: minimum support price for crops, minimum wage; government buying surplus
Case analysis: rent control or price ceiling on an Indian commodity
